Name: Tobii Pro Spectrum
Modes and specifications: Up to 1200 Hz; available modes depend on the configuration.
Description: A screen-based system for vision, cognition, and oculomotor research, with gaze sampling at up to 1200 Hz.
Applications: Microsaccades, reading, and gaze-contingent experiments
Editorial assessment: Temporal resolution is its main draw. Assess the complete setup, including synchronization hardware, experimental software, and tracking quality in your participant population.

Name: EyeLink 3
Modes and specifications: Up to 1000 Hz, depending on the operating mode.
Description: SR Research’s newer screen-based research system combines eye and head tracking at up to 1000 Hz, according to the manufacturer.
Applications: Head–eye coordination, reading, and cognitive science
Editorial assessment: The integrated design is worth evaluating. When migrating existing EyeLink experiments, check software versions, data fields, and end-to-end latency.

Name: Neon
Modes and specifications: NeonNet documentation lists gaze and eye-state data at 200 Hz; scene video is 30 Hz.
Description: Neon combines an eye-tracking module with interchangeable frames and provides gaze, pupil, and other eye-state signals.
Applications: Natural behavior, children, sports, and interaction prototypes
Editorial assessment: Calibration-free operation can reduce preparation time, but task-specific validation remains necessary. Evaluate cloud analysis, offline workflows, and data governance together.

Name: Tobii Pro Fusion
Modes and specifications: Up to 250 Hz; confirm the available modes and licenses.
Description: A screen-based eye tracker designed for deployment across research locations, with sampling at up to 250 Hz.
Applications: UX, reading, behavioral experiments, and field deployments
Editorial assessment: A useful option when deployment flexibility matters. Before choosing it, check licensed sampling modes, SDK access, and analysis-software costs.

Name: EyeLink 1000 Plus
Modes and specifications: Up to 2000 Hz binocularly with the head stabilized; Remote tracking typically supports up to 1000 Hz.
Description: Uses a dedicated Host PC and offers multiple mounts and lenses, with integration options for neurophysiological equipment.
Applications: Microsaccades and combined EEG, fMRI, or MEG experiments
Editorial assessment: Its strengths are experimental control and configuration flexibility. Specify head-stabilized or head-free tracking, lenses, mounts, and synchronization requirements in the purchase configuration.

Name: Tobii Pro Glasses 3
Modes and specifications: Confirm the 50 / 100 Hz modes against the specific version.
Description: A glasses-based system that combines first-person scene video with eye-tracking data for observing behavior beyond a monitor.
Applications: Consumer behavior, sports, human factors, and field research
Editorial assessment: Natural activities are the main use case. Trial dynamic area-of-interest annotation, prescription-lens options, and the video-analysis workflow before committing.

Name: Tobii Pro Spark
Modes and specifications: 60 Hz; sampling rate does not indicate spatial accuracy.
Description: Records gaze at 60 Hz and is positioned as an accessible system for attention and behavioral research.
Applications: Teaching, website UX, and attention analysis with large areas of interest
Editorial assessment: Useful for fixation distributions and dwell analysis. For fast saccade dynamics, first validate whether its temporal resolution meets the task requirements.

Name: Tobii Glasses X
Modes and specifications: No sampling-rate value is entered here without verification.
Description: A wearable in Tobii’s current product catalog, positioned for attention recording in UX, sports, and industrial environments.
Applications: Skill training, sports, and industrial tasks
Editorial assessment: Evaluate field deployment and visualization workflows first. Do not assume its raw-data interfaces are identical to those of Pro Glasses 3.

Name: EyeLink Portable Duo
Modes and specifications: Up to 2000 Hz binocularly with the head stabilized; up to 1000 Hz with the head free to move.
Description: A portable screen-based system with head-stabilized and head-free modes that uses the EyeLink experimental-software ecosystem.
Applications: Off-site experiments, schools, and data collection across locations
Editorial assessment: Especially relevant for teams with existing EyeLink programs. Portable does not mean recording while walking: a display and suitable participant positioning are still required.

Name: Pupil Core
Modes and specifications: Eye-camera rates and gaze-output rates differ; verify the hardware version.
Description: Modular head-mounted hardware works with open-source software, a network API, and Python plugins for programmable recording.
Applications: Research prototypes, method development, and custom integrations
Editorial assessment: Suited to developers who want control over acquisition. Allow time for calibration, camera adjustment, and maintaining your own analysis workflow.

Name: Pupil Invisible
Modes and specifications: Legacy product; Neon specifications must not be applied to it.
Description: Pupil Labs’ deep-learning eye-tracking glasses are now documented as a legacy platform replaced by Neon.
Applications: Reproducing existing datasets and comparing historical methods
Editorial assessment: Relevant when interpreting older studies. For used equipment, verify the companion phone, applications, cloud services, and maintenance status.

Name: Gazepoint GP3
Modes and specifications: Distinguish GP3 from GP3 HD and confirm the exact model.
Description: Gazepoint’s screen-based eye tracker comes with an associated analysis-software ecosystem and developer interfaces.
Applications: Teaching demonstrations, website testing, and basic attention studies
Editorial assessment: Run a pilot with your own display, participants, and area-of-interest sizes. Include the analysis-software edition and licensing in the budget.

Name: Smart Eye Pro
Modes and specifications: Depends on the cameras and system configuration; software version numbers are not sampling rates.
Description: A remote head- and eye-tracking system configurable with 2–8 cameras for more complex environments.
Applications: Driving, aviation, multiple displays, and control rooms
Editorial assessment: Worth evaluating for larger movement spaces and multiple display surfaces. Camera placement, calibration, and spatial mapping add engineering work compared with a single screen bar.

Name: Smart Eye AI-X
Modes and specifications: Confirm sampling rate and supported display size in the current configuration sheet.
Description: Smart Eye positions AI-X for screen-based studies in marketing, UX, and media.
Applications: Advertising, websites, and attention to media
Editorial assessment: Compare deployment workflows and the analysis ecosystem. Verify the raw outputs, synchronization options, and licenses required by your study.

Name: Smart Eye Aurora
Modes and specifications: Historical specifications are not treated as a single current configuration.
Description: Aurora is a compact remote tracker in Smart Eye’s product portfolio for screen-related research.
Applications: Screen-based studies and existing Smart Eye projects
Editorial assessment: Official product information remains available, but configurations may differ by generation. Ask about current availability, firmware, and support.

Name: Dikablis Glasses X
Modes and specifications: The website contains both 60 Hz and “up to 120 Hz” descriptions; no single verified gaze-sampling rate is assigned here.
Description: Dikablis Glasses X works with the Prophea.X workflow and emphasizes field, sports, and multimodal recording.
Applications: Driving, sports, occupational tasks, and human factors
Editorial assessment: Trial fit and synchronization with other sensors. The website’s eye- and scene-camera rate descriptions need to be checked separately against the data sheet.

Name: TRACKPixx3
Modes and specifications: Consult the data sheet for sampling rate and short- or long-range lens configurations.
Description: A system comprising a high-speed camera, infrared illumination, mounting hardware, and a VPixx control unit, configurable in LabMaestro.
Applications: Visual psychophysics, gaze feedback, and synchronized experiments
Editorial assessment: Particularly relevant to labs with VPixx hardware. Budget for the control unit, lens, mounting hardware, and display as well as the tracker.

Name: LiveTrack Lightning
Modes and specifications: Official documentation lists binocular recording at 500 Hz.
Description: LiveTrack Lightning provides 500 Hz video-based eye tracking and can be combined with CRS stimulus-presentation equipment.
Applications: Saccades, pupillometry, and visual psychophysics
Editorial assessment: Evaluate the complete stimulus-presentation and recording chain. Validate head-position requirements, real-time interfaces, and synchronization.

Name: ViewPoint EyeTracker
Modes and specifications: Up to 400 Hz applies to certain head-fixed configurations, not the entire product range.
Description: Arrington Research offers head-fixed, head-mounted, and custom-integration options; some configurations include ocular torsion measurements.
Applications: Vision experiments, torsion measurements, and custom integrations
Editorial assessment: The range of configurations offers flexibility, but price and performance depend on the specific system. Check older web specifications against the newer catalog item by item.

Name: Varjo XR-4 series
Modes and specifications: The manufacturer reports 200 Hz eye tracking; this is separate from display refresh rate.
Description: The XR-4 series uses eye tracking for dynamic foveated rendering in professional simulation and mixed-reality environments.
Applications: Flight simulation, design reviews, and XR research
Editorial assessment: Consider it when professional imaging and simulation integration matter. Evaluate the workstation, software licenses, and eye-tracking outputs available through the SDK.

Name: VIVE Focus Vision
Modes and specifications: Display refresh rate is not used as a proxy for eye-tracking sampling rate.
Description: VIVE Focus Vision integrates eye tracking and automatic IPD adjustment for compatible VR applications.
Applications: VR interaction, avatars, and foveated rendering
Editorial assessment: Confirm that the target application and operating mode expose the eye-tracking fields you need. Recalibration is required after changing IPD or headset position.

Name: VIVE Pro Eye
Modes and specifications: Older platform; availability and software support require confirmation.
Description: VIVE Pro Eye integrates eye tracking and has been used in VR interaction and gaze-related research.
Applications: Reproducing existing VR experiments and SDK-based research
Editorial assessment: Confirm stock and support status, then check whether SRanipal, OpenXR, or the application-level interface works in your target environment.

Name: FOVE 0
Modes and specifications: Eye cameras: 120 Hz. Display: 70 Hz. These are different rates.
Description: FOVE 0 provides eye-tracking data and SDKs for multiple languages, with Unity and Unreal integration options.
Applications: VR method development, gaze interaction, and analysis
Editorial assessment: Data interfaces are a main attraction. Display, positional tracking, and connection requirements also constrain experiment design, so trial the complete system.

Name: Pimax Crystal (original)
Modes and specifications: 120 Hz, according to documentation for the original model.
Description: The original Pimax Crystal supports automatic IPD and dynamic foveated rendering; official material lists 120 Hz eye tracking.
Applications: PC VR, simulation, and foveated rendering
Editorial assessment: Model identification is essential. This entry covers the original Crystal only and does not merge features from other Crystal products.

Name: Apple Vision Pro
Modes and specifications: No eye-tracking sampling rate is inferred from display refresh rate.
Description: Vision Pro uses infrared cameras and LEDs for eye interaction, with gaze serving as a core system input.
Applications: Spatial interaction, interface design, and user experience
Editorial assessment: System-level interaction does not establish access to research data. Ordinary apps do not receive continuous gaze data directly; check eligibility and restrictions for specialized interfaces.

Name: HoloLens 2
Modes and specifications: 90 Hz is an optional Extended Eye Tracking mode; the standard interface is approximately 30 Hz.
Description: HoloLens 2 provides a standard gaze ray and extended eye-tracking interfaces, with user permission and calibration required.
Applications: AR interaction, industrial tasks, and reproducing existing studies
Editorial assessment: The API mode determines the available data. Distinguish the standard approximately 30 Hz output from extended 30 / 60 / 90 Hz modes, and check the device lifecycle.

Name: PCEye
Modes and specifications: The official support page lists a gaze data rate of 33 Hz.
Description: PCEye connects over USB and works with TD Control to support eye-based control of a Windows computer.
Applications: Everyday computer access and assistive communication
Editorial assessment: Evaluate comfort, target selection, and sustained use. Research-data export capabilities require separate confirmation.

Name: TD Pilot
Modes and specifications: Check current official system and application compatibility information.
Description: TD Pilot combines eye access with the iPad platform for users who need assistive communication and device access.
Applications: iPad access and symbol- or text-based communication
Editorial assessment: Trial the actual communication software, mounting arrangement, and everyday portability. AAC devices and research trackers serve different evaluation goals.

Name: TD I-Series
Modes and specifications: Configurations vary across the series; no single sampling rate is assigned.
Description: TD I-Series combines a display, eye tracking, and communication functions in a dedicated device, with multiple sizes and configurations.
Applications: Text and symbol communication, and everyday computer access
Editorial assessment: Compare practical accessibility, mounts, speakers, and support. Clearly distinguish generations of I-Series and TD I-Series devices.

Name: HIRU
Modes and specifications: Confirm the compatibility list together with the required firmware.
Description: IRISBOND HIRU is a multiplatform eye-access device for compatible Windows and iPadOS environments.
Applications: Cross-platform assistive access and AAC
Editorial assessment: Check the exact iPad model, OS version, application support, and mounting position. Platform support does not mean every device is plug-and-play.

Name: Eyegaze Edge
Modes and specifications: The website lists Encore at 50 Hz and Prime at 60 Hz; these are not combined into a single device specification.
Description: Eyegaze Edge combines an eye-tracking camera, tablet, and communication functions, with different camera configurations available.
Applications: Sustained eye-controlled communication and device access
Editorial assessment: Confirm whether the configuration uses an Encore or Prime camera. Their working distances, monocular/binocular modes, and sampling rates differ and should be trialed separately.

Name: EyeOn series
Modes and specifications: No uniform sampling rate for the range has been verified from the overview page.
Description: EyeOn is an assistive communication tablet product line presented by EyeTech for communication and access across age groups.
Applications: AAC, everyday communication, and device access
Editorial assessment: Evaluate the communication tasks and support services. Ask the supplier to specify the eye-tracking hardware, applications, and data-export permissions.

Name: Tobii Eye Tracker 5
Modes and specifications: The page does not disclose research sampling modes suitable for direct comparison. Windows Eye Control is also unsupported.
Description: Tobii Eye Tracker 5 uses gaze and head movement to enhance interaction in supported PC games.
Applications: Driving and flight simulation games, and gaze overlays for streaming
Editorial assessment: The official page states that it is incompatible with Pro SDK / Pro Lab and is not licensed to collect eye-tracking research data by default. It is not a direct substitute for a research tracker.

Description: The GP3 HD 150 Hz model uses USB 3 for behavioral research and UX data collection.
Applications: UX, market research, and basic experiments

Description: 7invensun provides official aSee Pro user guides and safety documentation as part of its eye-movement analysis product range.
Applications: Research and teaching where Chinese-language support is useful

Modes and specifications: Check the exact model and firmware; this is a product-family entry.
Description: Official materials cover aSee Glasses, while the company’s site presents applications of aSee Glasses Plus.
Applications: Outdoor behavior, teaching, human factors, and mobile research
Editorial assessment: Chinese-language support and local implementation may be useful. Distinguish Glasses, Plus, and other generations rather than mixing their specifications.

Name: Vida / Vida Go
Modes and specifications: The manufacturer describes 60 Hz operation. Its stated 17 ms recovery time is not the same as end-to-end system latency.
Description: Powered by IntelliGaze 11, Vida is available as a Grid Pad module and through a standalone-camera option.
Applications: Grid communication and Windows access
Editorial assessment: Trial it in everyday postures and lighting. Clarify regional availability and the mounting configurations of Vida and Vida Go.

Name: Lumin-i
Modes and specifications: Confirm the hardware generation and the paired Grid Pad model.
Description: Lumin-i works with Grid Pad communication devices and is designed for sustained everyday eye access.
Applications: The Grid ecosystem and assistive communication
Editorial assessment: Prioritize tracking recovery, calibration, and target selection in real use instead of comparing nominal sampling rates alone.

Name: ST ONE
Modes and specifications: The official page lists eye tracking at 100 Hz and scene video at 30 FPS.
Description: ST ONE provides gaze, pupil, and eye-position data, with streaming and API access.
Applications: Mobile behavior, slippage studies, and programmable recording
Editorial assessment: Calibration reuse and resistance to slippage are manufacturer design priorities. Test offsets, data loss, and recovery with your participants and activities.

Name: ST ONE Light
Modes and specifications: The official announcement lists 100 FPS eye tracking. The image used here illustrates the ST ONE product family.
Description: The official ST ONE Light announcement emphasizes onboard image processing and connectivity with Android devices and PCs.
Applications: Mobile research, wearable interaction, and device integration
Editorial assessment: Onboard processing can reduce dependence on external computing. Confirm its relationship to ST ONE, available data fields, and actual availability before ordering.

Name: ST ART
Modes and specifications: The official page lists 50 Hz. Installation assumptions for a general-purpose screen tracker do not apply.
Description: ST ART integrates eye tracking into microscopes and other optical eyepiece devices to provide gaze and eye measurements.
Applications: Microscopy tasks, optical-device human factors, and gaze interaction
Editorial assessment: A specialized optical integration: check host-device interfaces, eyepiece dimensions, display overlays, and mapping to external video first.

Name: IntelliGaze / CAM30 series
Modes and specifications: The official support page requires IntelliGaze 11 for CAM30NXT. No single sampling rate is assigned to the entire range.
Description: alea technologies provides IntelliGaze for eye-based communication and Windows access, with several CAM30 hardware generations.
Applications: Assistive communication, Windows access, and eye-control activities
Editorial assessment: Hardware and software licenses need to match. Check the compatibility of CAM30NT, CAM30NXT, and each software version individually.

Name: AdHawk MindLink
Modes and specifications: The 2021 manufacturer announcement lists 500 samples per second. This launch specification does not establish a currently purchasable configuration.
Description: AdHawk MindLink uses MEMS eye sensing without eye-imaging cameras and was introduced as a research-oriented wearable.
Applications: Comparing wearable methods, low-power sensing, and reproducing existing studies
Editorial assessment: The sensing approach differs from video-based tracking. Evaluate data definitions, synchronization, and task suitability. The current manufacturer site could not be read reliably; availability and support need confirmation.

Name: Meta Quest Pro
Modes and specifications: Display refresh rate is not treated as eye-tracking sampling rate. Confirm current availability and support.
Description: Meta Quest Pro uses eye and facial signals for avatars and immersive interaction, with related developer interfaces.
Applications: VR social interaction, gaze interfaces, and reproducing existing studies
Editorial assessment: Check developer licensing, permissions, and SDK device support. This entry is retained as a historical platform; its launch page does not establish current inventory.

Name: PlayStation VR2
Modes and specifications: PS5 and PC support differ. Raw-data access and developer eligibility require separate verification.
Description: PlayStation VR2 uses eye information in supported PS5 content for gaze-related interaction and rendering.
Applications: Console VR, immersive experiences, and foveated-rendering examples
Editorial assessment: Sony explicitly states that headset eye tracking is not supported in PC mode. PC connectivity alone does not make it an open research eye tracker.
